clue.text: An outburst from Francesca, perhaps

indicators.note: 'from' says the letters are taken straight out of the words that follow

parts.note: the tail of the name runs on into the start of the next word

explanation.surface: Someone called Francesca, perhaps an opera heroine, is prone to sudden emotional eruptions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Francesca, perhaps' looks like a name being exemplified; the answer spans francESCA PErhaps.
explanation.definitionFit: An escape of gas or steam is a sudden release, a sense close to a burst or leak.

clue.text: Against ale being brewed in this part of England

indicators.note: brewing mixes ingredients together, so the letters are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A local objection to beer production in some English region.
explanation.walkthrough: East Anglia is the eastern bulge of England, Norfolk and Suffolk, a farming region.
explanation.definitionFit: East Anglia is a named region of eastern England, so it is a part of the country.

clue.text: Head, first to rumble practical joke

parts.note: a head is a headland, a promontory

indicators.note: 'first to' points at the opening letter of the word after it

explanation.surface: A leader is the first to see through a prank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' reads as a leader or verb, but it is a geographical headland.
explanation.definitionFit: A caper is a playful escapade or prank, a synonym for a practical joke.

clue.text: Governor, knight, raised capital

parts.note: guv'nor is slang for one's father

indicators.note: in a down light, raising a word sends it upwards, so it reads bottom to top

parts.note: Sir is the title of a knight

explanation.surface: A governor and a knight built up a city as a capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Governor' is old slang for one's father, hence PA.
explanation.definitionFit: Paris is the capital city of France.

clue.text: Injury caused by a jerk

parts.note: surface reading: harm done by an unpleasant, foolish person
setter's reading: a neck injury caused by a sudden jolt, as in a car crash

explanation.walkthrough: A 'jerk' sounds like an idiot, but here it is a sudden violent movement of the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Whiplash is the medical term for neck strain from a sharp back-and-forth snap.

clue.text: The boys save ten at sea — that's astonishing

indicators.note: being at sea means confused and lost, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A lifeboat crew rescues ten people at sea, a remarkable feat.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is an old-fashioned American exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavens to Betsy is an exclamation used when someone is astonished, like 'goodness me'.

clue.text: Stops meeting with professional villains

explanation.surface: Someone halts a gathering of experienced criminals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stops meeting' looks like someone avoiding a rendezvous; it means ending a parliamentary session.
explanation.definitionFit: To prorogue a parliament is to discontinue its session without dissolving it.

clue.text: See a fine aquatic bird, duck, over part of the day

parts.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
a duck is a score of nothing, shaped like zero
on and over both mean 'about', as in a row on or over money

explanation.surface: Birdwatchers spot a seabird and a duck flying over during the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' is the cricket score of nothing, giving the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: The afternoon is the stretch of the day between noon and evening.

clue.text: A lot of extremely energetic publicity

indicators.note: a lot of something is most but not all of it, so the end is cut off

explanation.surface: A great deal of very lively promotion for something.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the last letter of HYPER leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Hype is excessive promotional fuss, a word for intense publicity.

clue.text: Game of catch followed by rest

indicators.note: one part coming after another means the pieces are joined in that order

parts.note: to contract an illness is to catch it
in snooker a bridge, or rest, is a cue support

explanation.surface: A ball game where a catch is followed by a break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rest' sounds like a pause, but a snooker rest is also called a bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Contract bridge is the standard modern form of the card game bridge.

clue.text: The sort of star that could make pa nervous

indicators.note: 'could make' says the following letters can be reworked into something else

explanation.surface: A celebrity so dazzling that Dad gets jittery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star' suggests a celebrity, but it is an astronomical one.
explanation.definitionFit: A supernova is a star that explodes and briefly blazes with enormous brightness.

clue.text: Pensioner rings conservationists, available whenever needed

indicators.note: to ring something is to encircle it, so one piece goes around the other

parts.note: the National Trust, the UK heritage conservation charity

explanation.surface: A retiree phones an environmental group, always on call.
explanation.walkthrough: OAP is British shorthand for an old-age pensioner; the National Trust looks after historic houses and countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: Something on tap is readily available, like beer drawn straight from a cask.

clue.text: How chess players sit? It's the same for everyone

definitions.meaning: first meaning: literally facing each other over the board
second meaning: applying equally to all

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful literal reading of the idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: An across-the-board change applies universally, affecting every person or category alike.

clue.text: Where impoverished writers used to eat in London?

definitions.text: Where impoverished writers used to eat in London?

parts.words: Where impoverished writers used to eat in London?
parts.note: surface reading: a cheap London eatery for poor authors

parts.words: Where impoverished writers used to eat in London?
parts.note: setter's reading: the historic London street of hack writers, with 'eat' pointing to food slang in its name

explanation.walkthrough: Grub is slang for food, which makes 'eat' look literal; the street itself housed hack writers.
explanation.definitionFit: Grub Street was a London street famed for needy hack writers, and its name came to mean such writers.

clue.text: Doctor parked across a space

indicators.note: a car parked across something straddles it, so one piece sits around the other

explanation.surface: A medic leaves the car blocking a parking spot.
explanation.walkthrough: GP is the British term for a family doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: A gap is an empty space or opening between things.

clue.text: In favour of proposal suggesting publicity campaign

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
a motion is a formal proposal in a debate

explanation.surface: Backing a proposal that recommends an advertising drive.
explanation.definitionFit: Promotion is the marketing activity of advertising and publicising a product.

clue.text: Just pour lad bubbly with dishes of the day

indicators.note: something bubbly is fizzing and agitated, so the letters are churned up

explanation.surface: A waiter is told to serve champagne alongside the daily specials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bubbly' looks like champagne to pour, but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Plats du jour is French for the special dishes a restaurant offers on a given day.

clue.text: Messenger-boy committing crime in parish priest's house

indicators.note: 'in' places the crime inside the messenger-boy, one piece held within the other

parts.note: a page is a boy who runs errands
arson is the crime of fire-raising

explanation.surface: An errand boy commits an offence within a parish.
explanation.walkthrough: The page wraps around the arson.
explanation.definitionFit: A parsonage is the residence provided for a parish clergyman.

clue.text: Irish vegetables deserter stored as emergency food supply

indicators.note: something stored is kept inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a rat is someone who deserts a cause

explanation.surface: Irish produce with a runaway hidden in it, kept for a crisis.
explanation.walkthrough: The deserter goes inside the vegetables after IR.
explanation.definitionFit: Iron rations are small reserve packs of food carried by soldiers for emergencies.

clue.text: Return of Prohibition does for cop

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the word is read backwards

explanation.surface: Reintroducing the alcohol ban is enough for the police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cop' looks like a police officer noun, but it is the verb to catch.
explanation.definitionFit: To cop someone, in slang, is to seize or arrest them, the same as nab.

clue.text: NCO in court, so general worried

indicators.note: worried things are disturbed and unsettled, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A sergeant faces a court martial, and so a general is anxious.
explanation.definitionFit: A colour sergeant is a senior non-commissioned officer rank in British infantry and Royal Marines.

clue.text: Surly grumble made by Greek bird

explanation.surface: A bad-tempered complaint uttered by a Greek bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A growl is a low angry rumbling complaint, a surly grumble.

clue.text: A pair working in area in front of aircraft hangar

definitions.text: area in front of aircraft hangar

parts.note: PR is the abbreviation for pair
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: Two mechanics busy on the tarmac outside an aircraft shed.
explanation.definitionFit: The apron is the paved area at an airfield where aircraft are parked and serviced.

clue.text: Appear in diocese on the first of May

parts.note: a see is a bishop's diocese

indicators.note: 'the first of' keeps only the opening letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Someone is due to show up in a church district on May Day.
explanation.walkthrough: A bishop's see is his diocese, a churchy sense of a common word.
explanation.definitionFit: To seem is to appear to be something, a near-synonym.

clue.text: Musical — girl is full of it

indicators.note: something full of another thing holds it inside

explanation.surface: A self-centred girl thinks she is the star of the show.
explanation.walkthrough: Evita is the Lloyd Webber and Rice musical about Eva Perón, which neatly ties to the girl Eva.
explanation.definitionFit: Evita is a well-known stage musical about Argentina's Eva Perón.

clue.text: To hold a conversation in noisy nightclub sure is ridiculous

parts.note: a disco is a loud dance club

indicators.note: something ridiculous is absurd and makes no sense, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Trying to chat over the din of a club is a hopeless idea.
explanation.definitionFit: To discourse is to talk at length or converse, so it means holding a conversation.

clue.text: Short period surrounded by wealth in resort in California

indicators.note: being surrounded means being enclosed on all sides by the other piece
something short is lacking its end, so the last letter is cut

parts.note: a term is a period of time

explanation.surface: A brief stay among the rich at a Californian holiday town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' applies only to the period, and the shortened word then goes inside the wealth.
explanation.definitionFit: Monterey is a coastal resort town in California, famous for its bay.

clue.text: The Earth, perhaps, is flat — theory, initially

parts.note: a plane is a flat surface

indicators.note: 'initially' keeps only the opening letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A flat-earther's theory, stated at the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes the flat-earth claim, while 'perhaps' marks Earth as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Earth is one example of a planet, a body orbiting the Sun.
